name: The Kondo Effect
statement: Dilute magnetic impurities in a metal cause conduction-electron scattering that makes electrical resistivity rise, not fall, as temperature drops toward absolute zero.
statementAccent: makes electrical resistivity rise, not fall, as temperature drops
meaning: Normally a metal’s resistivity decreases as it cools, since lattice vibrations die down. The Kondo effect describes how a small concentration of magnetic impurities produces an anomalous resistance minimum at some low temperature, below which resistivity rises again as temperature is further reduced.
mechanism: Conduction electrons scatter off the localised spin of a magnetic impurity via an exchange interaction; Jun Kondo showed with third-order perturbation theory that this scattering grows logarithmically as temperature approaches zero, competing with the normal phonon-scattering decrease and producing the minimum. Below the characteristic Kondo temperature, conduction electrons collectively screen the impurity spin into a many-body singlet.

examples.text: The classic case is dilute iron impurities in gold, where a resistance minimum observed in the 1930s was later explained quantitatively by Kondo’s 1964 theory.
The effect appears in semiconductor quantum dots, where a single trapped electron spin acts as the impurity screened by electrons in attached leads, observable as a zero-bias conductance peak.

Compounds containing cerium or ytterbium exhibit dense-lattice versions of the Kondo effect, producing dramatically enhanced effective electron masses and, in some cases, unconventional superconductivity.

whyItMatters: The Kondo effect was the first solved example of a strongly correlated many-body problem in condensed-matter physics, motivating the renormalisation-group methods later used broadly, and it remains central to understanding heavy-fermion metals, quantum-dot transport, and correlated-electron materials.
limits: Kondo’s original perturbative calculation diverges at low temperature and cannot describe the full crossover to the singlet ground state; a complete solution required later non-perturbative work. The effect is specific to isolated, dilute magnetic moments — dense magnetic lattices or ordered magnetism change the physics.
misreadings: It is a misconception that any impurity causes a resistance minimum; the effect specifically requires impurities with an unquenched local magnetic moment, not just any scattering defect.
origin: Explained theoretically by Jun Kondo in 1964, building on an experimentally puzzling resistance minimum first observed in the 1930s and confirmed to be caused by magnetic impurities.

sources.text: Kondo effect, Wikipedia. — the resistivity minimum, Kondo’s 1964 theory, the Kondo temperature, and applications in quantum dots and heavy fermions.
"Kondo effect," Scholarpedia. — Kondo’s comparison of his theory with iron-in-gold experiments as the paradigmatic case.
